title: Interpreting two nipple-discharge patterns
keyOrderNotice: key shown first for review only; runtime options are randomized
reviewDisplayNote: Synthetic canonical profile; any patientName placeholder is rendered as Jamie Taylor for this review only.

before.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 42-year-old woman, visits the clinic after noticing intermittent small blood-stained spots inside the left side of the bra. Examination localizes the discharge to one duct. The discharge has appeared during ordinary activity as well as at the visit.
before.Task: Which feature of this nipple discharge most strongly supports a pathologic rather than a physiologic pattern?

after.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 42-year-old woman, visits the clinic after finding rust-coloured spots inside the left side of the bra between examinations. During the visit, compression produces pale fluid from several openings on each nipple; a reddish drop is also seen at one left-sided opening.
after.Task: Which interpretation best accounts for Jamie Taylor's nipple-discharge history?
Options: **KEY:** Pathologic left-sided episodes; physiologic expressed secretion
Physiologic left-sided episodes; physiologic expressed secretion
Endocrine-mediated left-sided episodes; endocrine-mediated expressed secretion

before: **KEY:** Spontaneous single-duct discharge
Uses the pattern that warrants pathologic-discharge evaluation; it does not identify a specific underlying lesion.
Intermittent episodes of discharge
Intermittent timing can seem reassuring or concerning, but does not classify the pattern as reliably as the origin and spontaneity.
Small volume of discharge
The amount can distract from the more informative pattern; scant discharge can still warrant evaluation.
after: **KEY:** Pathologic left-sided episodes; physiologic expressed secretion
Distinguishes the unilateral staining episodes from the bilateral secretion elicited during examination; one pattern need not explain every observation.
Physiologic left-sided episodes; physiologic expressed secretion
Overweights the bilateral expressed fluid and treats the separate left-sided history as reassuring.
Endocrine-mediated left-sided episodes; endocrine-mediated expressed secretion
Attributes the combined history to a systemic endocrine explanation because pale fluid can be expressed from both breasts, underweighting the focal reddish episodes.

inference: Separate two observed patterns and decide which interpretation accounts for both, rather than selecting an explicitly labelled feature.
focus: Confirm that the unprovoked left-sided history is sufficiently clear and that the endocrine interpretation is a credible competing error. The conceptual target remains pattern classification, not a specific breast lesion.
whatChanged: Replaced a single classic feature list with mixed raw observations. All three choices interpret both the between-examination episodes and the expressed secretion, with parallel grammar and credible overgeneralization errors.

companionVariants.whatChanged: Versioned the companion because its shared presentation changed; removed the redundant request-for-evaluation wording.

before.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 43-year-old woman, presents after thyroid FNA returned papillary thyroid carcinoma. No dedicated preoperative central or lateral neck-node mapping has been completed.
before.Current update: Neck ultrasound shows a 2 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma confined to one lobe, with no gross extension beyond the thyroid, no suspicious cervical nodes and a normal-appearing contralateral lobe. Staging has not identified distant metastases. The patient has chosen surgery and asks to preserve uninvolved thyroid tissue when an appropriate operation allows it.
before.Task: Which initial operation is most appropriate for Jamie Taylor's papillary thyroid carcinoma?

after.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 43-year-old woman, presents after thyroid FNA returned papillary thyroid carcinoma. No dedicated preoperative central or lateral neck-node mapping has been completed.
after.Current update: Neck ultrasound shows a 2 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma confined to one lobe, with no gross extension beyond the thyroid, no suspicious cervical nodes and a normal-appearing contralateral lobe. Staging has not identified distant metastases. The patient has chosen surgery.
after.Task: Which initial operation is most appropriate for Jamie Taylor's papillary thyroid carcinoma?

before: **KEY:** Lobectomy
Applies the confined unilateral tumor findings and tissue-preservation goal to an eligible initial operation.
Total thyroidectomy
A cancer diagnosis can prompt a more extensive operation, but that is less aligned with this eligible patient's stated tissue-preservation goal.
Subtotal thyroidectomy
Attempts a compromise on tissue preservation but is not the guideline's lobectomy-based initial approach for this profile.
after: **KEY:** Lobectomy
Applies the 2025 ATA initial-surgery recommendation to the stated unilateral 2 cm, intrathyroidal, node-negative and nonmetastatic profile.
Total thyroidectomy
Extends treatment beyond the recommended initial extent for this stated profile without another supplied indication for contralateral surgery.
Subtotal thyroidectomy
Treats subtotal resection as an intermediate cancer operation; it is not the recommended initial operation for this profile.

inference: Apply the disease-extent recommendation for initial surgery without using an explicit preference to identify the limited operation.
focus: Named clinician must confirm the ATA 2025 recommendation and absence of an alternative supplied indication for total thyroidectomy. The existing 2 cm observation is unchanged. No blanket rule for all thyroid cancers is taught.
whatChanged: Removed the tissue-preservation request entirely. Retained the selected-surgery status and staging facts; mapped the recommendation explicitly to current ATA guidance rather than relying on a preference to break a tie.

title: Reconciling perioperative antiretroviral instructions
keyOrderNotice: key shown first for review only; runtime options are randomized
reviewDisplayNote: Synthetic canonical profile; any patientName placeholder is rendered as Jamie Taylor for this review only.

before.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 43-year-old woman, visits the clinic before elective hernia repair at an outside surgical service. HIV is well controlled on a prescribed ritonavir-boosted antiretroviral regimen. The patient can swallow, and the prescribed medicines are available.
before.Task: Which perioperative antiretroviral medication plan is most appropriate for this elective operation?

after.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 43-year-old woman, visits the clinic before elective hernia repair at an outside surgical service. The clinic medication list records a ritonavir-boosted antiretroviral regimen being taken as prescribed. A generic preoperative instruction sheet includes these medicines among those to pause for the operation.
after.Task: Which perioperative antiretroviral plan should be sent to Jamie Taylor's surgical team?
Options: Withhold ritonavir and maintain the other agents

before: **KEY:** Keep the complete regimen
Recognizes feasible regimen continuity rather than repeating a stated permission to continue ART.
Suspend the complete regimen
Overgeneralizes perioperative medication withholding to an effective regimen that can be administered.
Omit the regimen's booster
Attempts to avoid interaction concerns by removing part of a regimen without coordinated review.
after: **KEY:** Continue the complete prescribed regimen
Reconciles the generic withholding instruction with the need to avoid an unnecessary interruption of a feasible prescribed regimen.
Interrupt the complete prescribed regimen
Applies a generic perioperative withholding instruction to ART without medication-specific review.
Withhold ritonavir and maintain the other agents
Attempts to reduce interaction concerns by removing ritonavir and continuing an incomplete regimen without coordinated review.

inference: Reconcile a generic stop instruction with regimen continuity, while recognizing that deleting a booster is a different error rather than a safe compromise.
focus: Confirm feasible administration and clinical plausibility of the instruction conflict without adding an unsupported fasting or drug-dosing rule. The companion separately tests a specific drug interaction; no new concept objective is intended.
whatChanged: Removed the permission-like swallowing/availability sentence and the generic well-controlled reassurance. Added a concrete conflicting instruction to interpret. Rebuilt three parallel plans around full continuity, blanket interruption and partial-regimen continuation; no filler or exact interruption interval.

companionVariants.whatChanged: Versioned the companion for the shared medication-reconciliation context; its interaction decision is unchanged.

clinicalMeaning: Stable concept objective retained; exact clinical equivalence requires named clinician review.

title: Recurrent peristomal skin injury
keyOrderNotice: key shown first for review only; runtime options are randomized
reviewDisplayNote: Synthetic canonical profile; any patientName placeholder is rendered as Jamie Taylor for this review only.

before.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 43-year-old woman, visits the clinic with burning around an ileostomy. Moist erosions form a ring around the stoma where effluent has contacted the skin. Skin farther out under the adhesive is intact. The stoma is viable, and the patient is well.
before.Current update: With the pouch removed, the nurse sees that the cutout extends beyond the stoma base and leaves the eroded ring exposed to effluent.
before.Task: Which appliance-care change should be made for Jamie Taylor's peristomal skin problem?
Options: **KEY:** Resize the opening to the stoma
Switch the adhesive to another product
Apply antifungal powder under the pouch
Increase the frequency of pouch changes

after.Presentation: Jamie Taylor, a 43-year-old woman, visits the clinic with recurrent burning around an ileostomy. Examination shows a moist red ring immediately beside the stoma, with intact skin farther out under the adhesive. The stoma is viable, and the patient feels well.
after.Current update: The removed barrier shows moisture around its inner edge, although the outer adhesive border remains attached.
after.Task: Which next step is most appropriate for Jamie Taylor's recurrent peristomal skin injury?
Options: **KEY:** Reassess pouch fit with the ostomy nurse
Switch to a different adhesive brand
Schedule more frequent routine pouch changes

before: **KEY:** Resize the opening to the stoma
Targets continued effluent contact at the observed fit problem with ostomy-nurse guidance.
Switch the adhesive to another product
Treats the injury as adhesive intolerance despite the intact more peripheral adhesive-contact skin and exposed-ring pattern.
Apply antifungal powder under the pouch
Treats a competing cause of peristomal rash without correcting the demonstrated exposure pathway.
Increase the frequency of pouch changes
Responds to wetness but leaves the opening-to-stoma mismatch in place.
after: **KEY:** Reassess pouch fit with the ostomy nurse
Uses the distribution and removed-appliance observations to prioritize assessment of the seal and fit before prescribing a particular product or opening dimension.
Switch to a different adhesive brand
Treats the complaint as an adhesive-product problem without first explaining the observed distribution and inner-edge moisture.
Start topical antifungal treatment
Treats a competing rash mechanism before assessing the appliance and the source of the recurrent contact injury.
Schedule more frequent routine pouch changes
May form part of an individualized plan, but selecting a new routine interval alone does not assess why this appliance repeatedly fails at the affected skin.

inference: Infer a recurrent appliance-contact problem from the skin distribution and removed-barrier observations, then choose fit assessment rather than an empiric product or interval change.
focus: Confirm a single best next step. The observations support assessment/refitting but do not establish an exact cutout defect, product choice or wear interval. Prior diagnosis feedback remains legitimate scaffolding.
whatChanged: Removed the explicit oversized-cutout mechanism and the presentation clause interpreting effluent contact. Used observable skin and barrier findings; the key now calls for assessment of fit, without assuming a demonstrated dimension that the vignette no longer supplies.

companionVariants.whatChanged: Versioned the companion because the shared presentation now contains raw morphology rather than a supplied effluent-contact explanation.

clinicalMeaning: Stable concept objective retained; exact clinical equivalence requires named clinician review.

title: Localizing an abdominal-wall hernia
keyOrderNotice: key shown first for review only; runtime options are randomized
reviewDisplayNote: Synthetic canonical profile; any patientName placeholder is rendered as Ella Morgan for this review only.

before.Presentation: Ella Morgan, a 6-year-old girl, visits the clinic with her mother, Rachel Morgan, who remains in the same room throughout the visit. Her mother points out a small focal lump in Ella's upper abdominal midline. Examination identifies a small abdominal-wall gap with protruding fat at that site, above the navel. Ella is comfortable.
before.Task: Which diagnosis best explains Ella Morgan's abdominal-wall lump?

after.Presentation: Ella Morgan, a 6-year-old girl, visits the clinic with her mother, Rachel Morgan, who remains in the same room throughout the visit. Her mother points out a small focal lump in Ella's upper abdominal midline. Examination identifies a small abdominal-wall gap with protruding fat at that site, above the navel. Her previous abdominal operation used a right-lower-quadrant incision. Ella is comfortable.
after.Task: Which diagnosis best explains Ella Morgan's abdominal-wall lump?

before: **KEY:** Epigastric hernia
Uses the location and focal fat-containing wall defect rather than absence of bulges elsewhere.
Umbilical hernia
Confuses a nearby midline location with the navel itself.
Inguinal canal hernia
Overgeneralizes a common pediatric hernia category without using the examination site.
after: **KEY:** Epigastric hernia
Uses the focal upper-midline fat-containing wall defect; the previous incision is at a different site.
Spigelian hernia
Confuses a lateral abdominal-wall defect near the semilunar line with the observed midline defect.
Incisional hernia
Overweights the operative history without matching the current defect to the prior incision.
Lumbar hernia
Confuses a posterior or flank wall defect with the anterior upper-midline finding.

inference: Localize the defect and relate it to the operative history among competing abdominal-wall hernias.
focus: Still an anatomical-recognition task, with stronger same-category competitors. Confirm pediatric plausibility. Morgagni is diaphragmatic and is excluded from this abdominal-wall option set; no new diagnosis or concept meaning is intended.
whatChanged: Replaced umbilical/inguinal competitors with Spigelian, incisional and lumbar hernias. Added the location of the prior incision as decision-critical raw history, without an option-by-option negative list. Morgagni is not used because its compartment differs.
clinicalMeaning: Stable concept objective retained; exact clinical equivalence requires named clinician review.
